questions.prompt: A feasible point \(x\) is stationary for a differentiable objective over a closed convex set when, for every step size \(t > 0\),
options: the projection of \(x\) is the origin
\(\nabla f(x)\) is a positive multiple of \(x\)
\(x\) equals the projection of \(x - t \nabla f(x)\)
\(x\) equals \(x - t \nabla f(x)\), even if that point lies outside the set
questions.explanation: Stationarity is the fixed point of a projected gradient step. If the trial point \(x - t \nabla f(x)\) leaves the set, the projection has to bring it back to the same \(x\). Accepting an infeasible trial point is an ordinary gradient step, not the constrained one. The origin and a sign condition on \(x\) are not the fixed-point test.

questions.prompt: Minimize \((x - 4)^2\) on \([0,\ 2]\), starting at \(0\), with step size \(1\). The gradient at \(0\) is \(-8\). What is the next iterate?
questions.explanation: The trial point is \(0 - 1 \cdot (-8) = 8\). Clipping \(8\) to \([0,\ 2]\) gives \(2\). Reporting \(8\) stops before the projection. Reporting \(-8\) is the gradient. Reporting \(0\) leaves the start unchanged. The right endpoint is the minimizer on this interval, and one projected step from the left endpoint reaches it.

questions.prompt: For a convex objective with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and a constant step \(0 < t \le 1/L\), the projected-gradient bound of order \(1/k\) controls
options: the number of vertices of the feasible set
the function gap \(f(x_k) - f^\star\)
the distance \(\lVert x_k - x^\star\rVert\)
the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian
questions.explanation: The standard estimate is \(f(x_k) - f^\star \le \lVert x_0 - x^\star\rVert^2 / (2 t k)\). The quantity on the left is the function gap. The distance to a minimizer need not fall like \(1/k\) unless a stronger hypothesis, such as strong convexity, is added. The bound does not count vertices and does not claim a Hessian eigenvalue.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order of one projected-gradient iteration. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The trial point uses the gradient, so the gradient is first. The projection uses the trial point. The replacement uses the projection. Projecting the current point before the gradient step does nothing when the current point is already feasible, and it is not a swap of these four steps.

steps: Evaluate the gradient at the current feasible point.
Subtract the step size times that gradient from the current point, producing a trial point.
Project that trial point onto the feasible set.
Replace the current point by that projection.

questions.prompt: On the unit square, take one projected step of length \(1\) for the objective \(x\), whose gradient is \((1,\ 0)\). Which points are fixed by that step?
questions.explanation:
The trial point is \((x - 1,\ y)\), then each coordinate is clipped to \([0,\ 1]\).
• From \((0,\ 0)\), \((0,\ 1)\), and \((0,\ 1/4)\) the trial has first coordinate \(-1\), and clipping returns the same point.
• From \((1,\ 0)\) the trial is \((0,\ 0)\), whose projection is \((0,\ 0)\).
• From \((1/2,\ 1/2)\) the trial is \((-1/2,\ 1/2)\), whose projection is \((0,\ 1/2)\).
The fixed points are the minimizers, the left edge of the square.

questions.prompt: For the scalar objective \(\tfrac12 a t^2 + b t\), a step of length \(s\) forms a trial point before projection. That trial point equals
questions.explanation: The gradient is \(a t + b\). The trial point subtracts \(s\) times that gradient from \(t\). Every name appears. Adding the gradient steps uphill. Dropping \(s\) uses a unit step that the formula does not assume. Using \(a t - b\) flips the linear term.

questions.prompt: A note takes one projected step for \((x - 3)^2 + (y - 1)^2\) on the unit square, starting at \((0,\ 0)\) with step size \(1/2\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The partial derivatives are \(2(x - 3)\) and \(2(y - 1)\), so the gradient at the origin is \((-6,\ -2)\). Subtracting half of that gradient lands at \((3,\ 1)\). The unit square is the stated set. The trial point is outside it. Clipping gives \((1,\ 1)\), which is the next iterate. Accepting \((3,\ 1)\) skips the projection.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 260 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a shaded quadrant</title><line x1="48" y1="168" x2="236" y2="168"/><polygon points="236,168 229.6,170.7 229.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="180" x2="48" y2="24"/><polygon points="48,24 50.7,30.4 45.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="230" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><rect x="48" y="48" width="150" height="120" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/></svg>
steps: The feasible set is the unit square \([0,\ 1] \times [0,\ 1]\).
The next iterate is the trial point \((3,\ 1)\).
reasons: The trial point \((3,\ 1)\) is outside the square. The next iterate is its projection \((1,\ 1)\).
The gradient at the origin is not \((-6,\ -2)\).
The arithmetic from \((0,\ 0)\) and step \(1/2\) does not produce \((3,\ 1)\).

questions.prompt: The projected-gradient theorem says that the function gap is at most \(\lVert x_0 - x^\star\rVert^2 / (2 t k)\) when its hypotheses hold. With \(\lVert x_0 - x^\star\rVert^2 = 16\), \(t = 1/2\), and \(k = 4\), what is that upper bound?
questions.explanation: The denominator is \(2 \cdot (1/2) \cdot 4 = 4\). The bound is \(16/4 = 4\). This number upper-bounds \(f(x_k) - f^\star\). It is not a measurement of \(\lVert x_k - x^\star\rVert\). Reporting \(16\) stops before the division. Reporting \(8\) uses \(t k\) without the factor \(2\). Reporting \(2\) uses \(t = 1/2\) as if it were the whole denominator.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.prompt: When the feasible set is all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), one projected-gradient step
options: reduces to the ordinary gradient step \(x - t \nabla f(x)\)
still clips every coordinate to \([-1,\ 1]\)
calls a linear minimization oracle over a simplex
sets the gradient to zero for every objective in one iteration
questions.explanation: The projection onto the whole space is the identity, so the trial point is accepted. Clipping to a box is a different feasible set. A linear minimization oracle is the conditional-gradient step, not this one. One gradient step zeroes the gradient only for special objectives, such as a quadratic whose Newton step happens to match.

questions.prompt: Summing the decrease of projected steps with \(0 < t \le 1/L\), for a convex objective with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, produces
options: a quadratic bound on \(\lVert x_k - x^\star\rVert\) for every convex objective
finite termination on every quadratic
an increase of the objective at every accepted step
a function-gap bound of order \(1/k\)
questions.explanation: Each accepted step decreases the objective by a multiple of the squared movement, as the sufficient-decrease lemma does in the unconstrained case. Adding those decreases and using convexity bounds the gap by a constant over \(k\). A quadratic distance bound needs strong convexity. Finite termination is a conjugate-direction fact, not a projected-gradient fact. The step is built to decrease the objective when \(t \le 1/L\).
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.prompt: Minimize \(3x^2\) on \([-2,\ 2]\), starting at \(1\), with step size \(1\). The derivative at \(1\) is \(6\). What is the next iterate?
questions.explanation: The trial point is \(1 - 1 \cdot 6 = -5\). Clipping \(-5\) to \([-2,\ 2]\) gives \(-2\). Reporting \(-5\) is the trial point, which is outside the interval. Reporting \(1\) skips the step. Reporting \(6\) is the derivative. The second derivative is \(6\), so this step size is longer than \(1/L\). The iteration is still well defined, and the projection is what brings the trial point back to the endpoint.

questions.prompt: If the trial point \(x - t \nabla f(x)\) already lies in the feasible set, the projected update
options: rejects the step and stays at \(x\)
replaces the gradient by its negative before moving
equals that trial point
jumps to a farthest vertex instead
questions.explanation: The projection of a feasible point is itself, so the update is the ordinary gradient step. A vertex step is the conditional-gradient method. The step is rejected only by a line search that tests decrease, not by feasibility of the trial point. The gradient is already subtracted; flipping it again would reverse the direction.
